claim: Nucleosomes restrict the occupancy of most transcription factors by reducing binding and accelerating dissociation.
source: Nucleosomes restrict the occupancy of most transcription factors (TF) by reducing binding and accelerating dissociation, while a small group of TFs have high affinities to nucleosome-embedded sites and facilitate nucleosome displacement.
evidence: This is a general statement about nucleosome-TF interactions that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript (e.g., Luo et al., 2014b) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A small group of TFs have high affinities to nucleosome-embedded sites and facilitate nucleosome displacement.
source: Nucleosomes restrict the occupancy of most transcription factors (TF) by reducing binding and accelerating dissociation, while a small group of TFs have high affinities to nucleosome-embedded sites and facilitate nucleosome displacement.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript for Reb1 and Cbf1, as well as citations to prior work on pioneer factors.

claim: Reb1 and Cbf1 bind to their sites within nucleosomes with similar binding affinities as to naked DNA.
source: We show that these factors bind to their sites within nucleosomes with similar binding affinities as to naked DNA, trapping a partially unwrapped nucleosome without histone eviction.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by EMSA and FRET data shown in Figures 1 and 2, with specific S1/2 values reported.

claim: Reb1 and Cbf1 trap a partially unwrapped nucleosome without histone eviction.
source: We show that these factors bind to their sites within nucleosomes with similar binding affinities as to naked DNA, trapping a partially unwrapped nucleosome without histone eviction.
evidence: This is supported by FRET experiments showing decreased FRET efficiency upon Reb1/Cbf1 binding (Figure 2) and EMSA data showing the complex contains both DNA and histones (Figure 1).

claim: The binding and dissociation rates of Reb1 and Cbf1 are significantly slower at nucleosomal sites relative to those for naked DNA.
source: Both the binding and dissociation rates of Reb1 and Cbf1 are significantly slower at the nucleosomal sites relative to those for naked DNA, demonstrating that the high affinities are achieved by increasing the dwell time on nucleosomes in order to compensate for reduced binding.
evidence: This is directly supported by single-molecule PIFE and FRET measurements presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5, showing specific kinetic rates.

claim: Reb1 and Cbf1 achieve high affinities to nucleosomes by increasing the dwell time on nucleosomes to compensate for reduced binding.
source: Both the binding and dissociation rates of Reb1 and Cbf1 are significantly slower at the nucleosomal sites relative to those for naked DNA, demonstrating that the high affinities are achieved by increasing the dwell time on nucleosomes in order to compensate for reduced binding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic data showing that the reduction in koff compensates for the reduction in kon, maintaining similar overall affinity.

claim: Reb1 shows slow migration rate in yeast nuclei.
source: Reb1 also shows slow migration rate in the yeast nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 7, demonstrating a half-life of 25.8 ± 2.5 s for Reb1.

claim: The properties of Reb1 and Cbf1 are similar to those of human pioneer factors.
source: These properties are similar to those of human pioneer factors (PFs), suggesting that the mechanism of nucleosome targeting is conserved from yeast to humans.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data on human pioneer factors (Cirillo and Zaret, 1999; Sekiya et al., 2009) and the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of nucleosome targeting is conserved from yeast to humans.
source: These properties are similar to those of human pioneer factors (PFs), suggesting that the mechanism of nucleosome targeting is conserved from yeast to humans.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the similarity of properties between yeast factors (Reb1, Cbf1) and human pioneer factors.

claim: The fundamental unit of chromatin is the nucleosome, approximately 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins.
source: The fundamental unit of chromatin is the nucleosome,~147 base pairs (bp) of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the citation to Luger et al., 1997.

claim: Extensive contacts between nucleosomal DNA and the histone octamer suppress access to DNA-binding proteins, including many transcription factors.
source: Extensive contacts between nucleosomal DNA and the histone octamer suppress access to DNA-binding proteins, including many transcription factors (TFs) (Wolffe, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation to Wolffe, 1992.

claim: TFs take advantage of dynamic nucleosome structural fluctuations, which transiently expose DNA-binding sites for TF binding.
source: To overcome this steric occlusion, TFs take advantage of dynamic nucleosome structural fluctuations, which transiently expose DNA-binding sites for TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Widom, 2004 and Polach and Widom, 1995, describing the site exposure mechanism.

claim: The site exposure mechanism results in reduced TF occupancy relative to that on naked DNA, since the TF can bind only when the site is partially unwrapped.
source: However, this site exposure mechanism (Li and Widom, 2004; Polach and Widom, 1995) results in reduced occupancy relative to that on naked DNA, since the TF can bind only when the site is partially unwrapped.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the site exposure model, supported by citations.

claim: Nucleosomes increase TF dissociation rates by orders of magnitude.
source: In addition, it was recently shown that nucleosomes increase TF dissociation rates by orders of magnitude (Luo et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014b.

claim: The decreased binding and increased dissociation rates can result in a reduction in the apparent dissociation constant for nucleosome substrates of over a 1000-fold.
source: In combination, the decreased binding and increased dissociation rates can result in a reduction in the apparent dissociation constant for nucleosome substrates of over a 1000-fold.
evidence: This is supported by the example of Gal4 binding provided in the next sentence and by citation to Luo et al., 2014b.

claim: Gal4 binds to its DNA target site at picomolar concentrations.
source: For example, Gal4 binds to its DNA target site at picomolar concentrations (Liang et al., 1996) whereas it requires nanomolar concentrations to bind nucleosomal DNA (Luo et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liang et al., 1996.

claim: Gal4 requires nanomolar concentrations to bind nucleosomal DNA.
source: For example, Gal4 binds to its DNA target site at picomolar concentrations (Liang et al., 1996) whereas it requires nanomolar concentrations to bind nucleosomal DNA (Luo et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014b.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors access their binding sites within nucleosomes as efficiently as they access fully exposed DNA without the aid of additional factors.
source: In contrast to TFs such as Gal4, pioneer transcription factors (PFs) access their binding sites within nucleosomes as efficiently as they access fully exposed DNA without the aid of additional factors (Zaret and Carroll, 2011).
evidence: This is a defining property of pioneer factors, supported by citation to Zaret and Carroll, 2011.

claim: Pioneer factors are thought to allow targeting of closed chromatin and to prime transcription activation.
source: This property is thought to allow PFs to target closed chromatin and to prime transcription activation (Iwafuchi-Doi and Zaret, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwafuchi-Doi and Zaret, 2014.

claim: In budding yeast, chromatin is mainly opened by a few highly expressed TFs that can access their nucleosome-embedded binding sites in the genome and establish local nucleosome depleted regions.
source: In budding yeast, chromatin is mainly opened by a few highly expressed TFs that can access their nucleosome-embedded binding sites in the genome and establish local nucleosome depleted regions (NDRs) (Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2018.

claim: Reb1 is a factor essential for yeast viability.

claim: Most of the Reb1-binding sites in the genome reside in NDRs.

If Reb1 achieves a higher binding affinity to nucleosomes by interacting with the exposed histone surface, this reduction in exposed histone octamer surface would reduce the affinity of Reb1 at the P3 position.
